newsitem.title: UK: U.S. green laws to maintain pressure on refiners.
newsitem.headline: U.S. green laws to maintain pressure on refiners.

text.p: Tough new green laws will maintain financial pressures on U.S. oil refiners by further fragmenting the industry's petroleum product mix, John van Meter, president of refiner Ashland International, said on Tuesday.

But growing demand, particularly from the renewed trend for large gas-guzzling private vehicles, should allow refiners satisfactory returns in the years to come, van Meter told the Oil and Money conference.
"The U.S. refining industry has been exceptionally competitive during the 1990s and has also been a bit of a puzzle.
"Refinery utilisation rates are high and demand is strong, two factors that normally point to healthy profits. Refinery margins have been poor and profitability has been low," van Meter said.
"Since 1992 the industry's product mix has become much more fragmented."
Van Meter said the huge costs associated with the 1992 U.S. Clean Air Act was the biggest factor behind the current poor profitability, and many refineries had closed at least partially as a result.
"But many other refiners opted to debottleneck or increase conversion capacity," he added.
As a result reforming capacity had been boosted.
"In short the industry simply has the capabilty to produce more product than the market demands -- even though demand has been strong and surplus capacity may be small."

Van Meter said a second and third phase of the Clean Air Act in 1998 and 2000 would not necessarily mean huge new investments. He said gasoline imports to the U.S., up 37 percent since 1992 to 360,000 barrels per day, had contributed to weaker refienry margins.
